t.1.42.1: The Sūta said: Having heard this, Jaratkāru, overcome by pain and sorrow, spoke out of grief to his own ancestors in a voice choked with tears.
t.1.42.3: The ancestors said: Son, by good fortune you have come to this place by chance. And why, O brahmin, have you not taken a wife?
t.1.42.2: I myself am Jaratkāru, your sinful son. Inflict that punishment upon me, the evil-doer whose self is undisciplined.
t.1.42.4: O fathers, this purpose ever turns about in my heart: that, remaining chaste with my seed drawn upward, I might carry this body to the world beyond.
t.1.42.5: But having seen you, sirs, hanging thus like birds, I have turned my mind away from celibacy, O grandfathers.
t.1.42.6: I will fulfil your cherished wish and I will marry, there is no doubt about this, if I ever find a maiden who bears the same name as mine.
t.1.42.7: And whatever maiden there may be who is offered of her own accord, like alms, her I will accept, provided she is one whom I shall not have to support.
t.1.42.9: Having spoken thus to his ancestors, the sage wandered over the earth, but he did not obtain a wife, O Śaunaka, for people thought, "This man is old."
t.1.42.8: Such a thing I would do, if I could obtain a marriage of that kind; otherwise I shall not do it. This is the truth, O grandfathers.
t.1.42.10: When he had fallen into despondency and had likewise been urged on by his ancestors, he went into the forest and, deeply grieved, cried out loudly.
t.1.42.11: Whatever beings exist here, both unmoving and moving, and those that are hidden from sight, let them all hear my words.
t.1.42.12: While I was engaged in fierce austerity, my ancestors, stricken with sorrow, urged me, saying, "Take a wife!" And so, out of a wish to do what is dear to them, I speak.
t.1.42.13: Seeking marriage, I wander over the whole earth begging for a maiden as alms, sirs; poor and accustomed to suffering, I have been enjoined to this by my ancestors.
t.1.42.14: Whatever being has a daughter, may those whom I have here called upon give their daughter to me as I wander in every direction.
t.1.42.15: The maiden who bears the same name as mine, who would be offered to me like alms, and whom I would not have to support: give me that maiden.
t.1.42.17: Having heard their words, that lord of the Nāgas, the serpent, took that richly adorned maiden and went into the forest, into his presence.
t.1.42.16: Then those serpents who had been set to keep watch on Jaratkāru took that news and reported it to Vāsuki.
t.1.42.18: There, O brahmin, Vāsuki, lord of the Nāgas, gave that maiden as alms to the great-souled one, but he did not accept her.
t.1.42.19: Thinking, “She may not bear the same name as mine,” and with the matter of her maintenance not yet considered, he, though firmly set on liberation, was torn in two minds about accepting her as his wife.
t.1.42.20: Then, O delight of the Bhṛgus, he asked the maiden's name, and he said, "Vāsuki, I shall not undertake her maintenance."
